analysis.one_liner: Requires government safety approval and public disclosure before genetically engineered foods and animals can be sold.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in June 2004 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2005, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, companies voluntarily consult the FDA before selling genetically engineered foods, and no formal approval is required. This bill would have changed that: companies would have to submit safety data, the public could see the applications and comment for at least 45 days, and the government could test foods, monitor approved products after sale, and order recalls. Genetically engineered animals would be regulated like new animal drugs, with environmental reviews. Products already on the market would be grandfathered in unless regulators later found new safety concerns.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who want to know what is in their food and want an independent government safety check before genetically engineered foods and animals reach grocery shelves. Farmers and food companies that do not use genetic engineering would also gain from stricter rules preventing unapproved or restricted genetically engineered crops from mixing into the general food supply, since the bill required segregation protocols, surveillance, and recall authority for restricted products.

how_it_helps.text: Producers must obtain premarket approval before selling any genetically engineered food in interstate commerce, replacing today's voluntary consultation system.
Applications and supporting research must be made public, with at least a 45-day public comment period, except for narrowly defined trade secrets; safety test results can never be withheld.

HHS must run programs to test foods for genetically engineered ingredients at every stage from farm to store, monitor the safety of approved products after they go on sale, and maintain a public registry of approved genetically engineered foods.

Genetically engineered animals and the techniques used to create them would be regulated as new animal drugs, requiring environmental assessments and giving the Secretary recall and suspension authority.
Unapproved genetically engineered foods or animals would be deemed adulterated, and the Secretary could order recalls of restricted products that leak into the food supply.

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural biotechnology and seed companies, which would bear the cost of formal applications, public disclosure of research, post-market monitoring, and possible recalls. Food companies using genetically engineered ingredients could face added costs from segregation and testing requirements. Some of these costs could ultimately show up in food prices.

drawbacks.text: The transition provision grandfathers every genetically engineered food and animal already in commerce: they are treated as approved unless the Secretary affirmatively finds new scientific information requires an application within two years, so the bill would not re-review the products already on shelves.

Formal premarket approval, public disclosure of research data, and testing programs would add regulatory costs and approval delays for agricultural biotechnology developers, which could slow the introduction of beneficial products and fall hardest on smaller developers.
The bill authorizes 'such sums as are necessary' in new spending for FDA testing, monitoring, and registry programs, an open-ended cost to taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give consumers an independent, transparent safety review and recall authority that today's voluntary consultation system lacks, at a real but conventional regulatory cost to biotech and food companies. Its biggest weakness is design, not intent: the grandfather clause exempts all existing genetically engineered products from the new approval process unless regulators later find new safety concerns, so the strongest protections would apply mainly to future products. The open-ended appropriation and the burden on smaller developers are fair criticisms, but the core trade-off is public transparency and mandatory safety review versus industry compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2004, referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the Genetically Engineered Foods Act on June 17, 2004.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, where no further action was taken.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill expired without a committee hearing, a floor vote, or any action in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The agricultural biotechnology industry is better off, since it avoided mandatory premarket approval, public disclosure of safety research, and recall exposure. Consumers did not get the independent safety review and transparency the bill would have provided.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Genetically Engineered Foods Act and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: 108th Senate
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill; no senator cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill would replace voluntary FDA consultation with mandatory premarket approval, public disclosure of safety research, post-market monitoring, and recall authority. Its interest in stopping the bill runs against consumers' interest in independent safety review.

industries.industry: Food manufacturers using genetically engineered ingredients
industries.note: Segregation protocols, tolerance rules for cross-mixing, and marketplace testing could raise compliance costs for companies handling genetically engineered commodities, while also reducing the risk of unapproved traits entering the food supply.

Genetically engineered animals and the techniques to produce them would be regulated as new animal drugs, with environmental assessments, public comment, and recall and suspension authority, requirements that did not otherwise exist.
